mathematics.independent_solution: In a strict convex polygon only two extreme parallel supporting lines can carry sides in any direction, one side per line since flat corners are excluded. Each parallel pair uses two unique sides, so at most floor(n/2) pairs. Sealed independent convex coordinate witnesses attain 1/2 for n=4,5 and 1/2/3 for n=6; zero for each is attained by cyclically joining the first n points (x,x^2), x=1,2,4,8,16,32, whose edge slopes including the closing edge are distinct binary sums. Thus possible sets are {0,1,2},{0,1,2},{0,1,2,3}. A half-turn of a simple genuine-corner polygon permutes vertices without fixed corners: a fixed corner at the center would have opposite collinear incident edges, a prohibited flat corner. All vertex orbits have size two, so odd n cannot have a center, even for concave simple polygons. Even n alone does not guarantee symmetry.

option_checks.proof: The sealed strictly convex 4/1 trapezoid has one pair, the 5/2 chamfered-rectangle witness has two, and the 6/1 witness has one, refuting 2/0/3 as fixed shape-independent counts.
The extreme-support bound gives maxima 2/2/3, and all sealed convex witnesses plus the zero-pair parabola family attain every nonnegative count through those maxima.
A strict convex pentagon cannot have three parallel pairs: pairs use disjoint sides and would need at least six sides. Its quadrilateral and hexagon upper bounds are right.

The strict convex trapezoid (0,0),(4,0),(3,2),(1,2) has opposite-vertex midpoints (1.5,1) and (2.5,1), so no single center. The 6/1 witness also cannot have a center, since a central half-turn would pair all six sides into three parallel pairs. The pentagon no-center clause alone is right.

Central symmetry pairs every nonflat corner into a two-member orbit. A fixed corner would force collinear opposite incident sides, excluded by the domain. Hence a simple polygon with odd corner count has no center, whether convex, concave or regular.
